meta.title: Who originally recorded "Red Red Wine"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not a UB40 original. "Red Red Wine" was written and first recorded by Neil Diamond in 1967 on Bang Records. UB40’s 1983 reggae version is a cover — and the band didn’t even realise Diamond wrote it.
meta.ogDescription: Everyone thinks it’s a UB40 song. It’s a 1967 Neil Diamond single — written and first recorded by him — that UB40 covered sixteen years later, thinking it was a Jamaican reggae tune.

answer.label: Not a UB40 original — a 1967 Neil Diamond single
answer.sourceLine: This is a near-total cover-eclipse: almost everyone hears ‘Red Red Wine’ as a UB40 song, but UB40’s 1983 reggae version is a cover. The song was written and first recorded by Neil Diamond in 1967 for Bang Records. UB40 found it not through Diamond but through Tony Tribe’s 1969 reggae cover — and famously didn’t realise Diamond had written it at all.

docMeta.dd: 1967 (Bang Records) — on Just for You, US No. 62

trail: The song was written and first recorded by Neil Diamond in 1967 for Bang Records, appearing on his album Just for You; it reached No. 62 on the US Billboard Hot 100 Wikipedia ↗.
In 1969 the Jamaican singer Tony Tribe recorded a reggae version for Trojan Records, which reached No. 46 in the UK. It was this version, not Diamond’s, that UB40 knew and set out to cover.

UB40’s 1983 reggae cover, from Labour of Love, went to No. 1 in the UK and — on a 1988 US re-release — No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, so thoroughly overtaking the original that Diamond’s authorship dropped out of public memory SecondHandSongs ↗.

authors.name: Neil Diamond
authors.kicker: The original recording artist and writer
authors.heading: About Neil Diamond
authors.bio: Neil Diamond (b. 1941) is one of the best-selling American singer-songwriters of all time, behind ‘Sweet Caroline’, ‘Cracklin’ Rosie’ and dozens more. He both wrote and first recorded ‘Red Red Wine’ in 1967, a modest hit that reached No. 62. There is a neat irony to it: he is the author and the original artist, yet the song is so bound up with UB40’s reggae arrangement that Diamond himself now often performs it that way.

authors.name: UB40
authors.heading: Why it gets pinned on UB40
authors.bio: UB40 released their reggae cover of ‘Red Red Wine’ in 1983 on Labour of Love, and it became so definitive that it eclipsed the 1967 original completely. The band knew the song only through Tony Tribe’s reggae version, not Diamond’s — guitarist Astro told the Financial Times that when they saw the writing credit ‘N Diamond’, they assumed it was a Jamaican artist called Negus Diamond. Their version is genuinely theirs; the only error is thinking the song began with them.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a clean cover-eclipse with a twist: nothing about UB40’s record is wrong, and the band themselves were the first to misattribute it. The error is believing they — or reggae — originated a song a Brill Building songwriter wrote in 1967.

items.why: Diamond’s version reached only No. 62, and the reggae arrangement UB40 gave it was so distinct that the pop original faded from memory entirely.

misattribution.truthLine: Written and first recorded by Neil Diamond in 1967, routed through Tony Tribe’s 1969 reggae cover, and made famous — but not originated — by UB40 in 1983 the record ↗.

context.heading: Why the cover ate the original
lead: A cover eclipses its original most completely when it transforms the song. Neil Diamond’s 1967 ‘Red Red Wine’ is a wistful pop ballad; UB40 rebuilt it as skanking reggae, and the new arrangement was so much more famous than the old one that it became the song, with the pop original nowhere in the public’s ear.

The strangest part is that the band who erased the original never knew it existed. UB40 covered a cover — Tony Tribe’s 1969 reggae version — and mistook the writer’s credit for a reggae artist’s name. The misattribution ran through the very people who made the song famous.
detailsBody: Neil Diamond writes and records it, 1967 (Bang Records); US No. 62.
Tony Tribe cuts a reggae version, 1969 (Trojan); UK No. 46.
UB40 cover Tony Tribe’s version, 1983 (Labour of Love) → UK No. 1.
A 1988 US re-release takes UB40’s version to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Diamond’s 1967 original all but disappears from public memory.
context.pull: UB40 covered a cover, and mistook the writer’s credit for a reggae artist’s name.
